case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Louisiana’s COVID-era emergency-liability immunity statute (LHEPA) can be applied in state court to heighten the fault standard and effectively bar private federal disability-discrimination claims under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Louisiana Health Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA) immunity provisions (gross-negligence / willful-misconduct threshold during declared public health emergency), and federal antidiscrimination statutes: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (including federal remedial limits as construed by Supreme Court precedent).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues Louisiana courts improperly imported LHEPA’s heightened state-law immunity/culpability standard (gross negligence or willful misconduct) into federal ADA/RA causes of action, thereby altering the elements and enforcement of federal civil rights claims; under the Supremacy Clause, a state emergency-immunity regime cannot displace or narrow federally created rights and remedies, and applying LHEPA here—where the alleged discrimination involved denial of aquatic therapy during the pandemic—produces “absurd” results and undermines uniform national enforcement of disability-rights law.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue certiorari should be denied because, regardless of LHEPA, petitioner’s requested relief is legally unavailable: compensatory emotional-distress damages are not recoverable in a private action under § 504 after Cummings, and Title III of the ADA does not permit private damages at all; additionally, petitioner’s pleadings fail to state facts showing the heightened misconduct needed to overcome LHEPA immunity, and the state courts correctly treated LHEPA as broadly applicable during the declared emergency with no textual limitation that would support preemption in this posture.
key_precedents: Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. ___ (2022) (emotional distress damages unavailable under Spending Clause statutes such as § 504)
Mills v. Hartford Healthcare Corp., 347 A.3d 605 (Conn. 2023) (state COVID-immunity interpretation example)
Resurgens, LLC v. Ervin, 894 S.E.2d 408 (Ga. 2023) (state COVID-immunity interpretation example)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor forcefully argue that LHEPA was applied as a heightened fault prerequisite to federal liability, which would raise serious reverse-Erie/Supremacy Clause concerns if it actually defeated a federally authorized claim for available relief. But Justice Barrett’s and Justice Thomas’s narrower point is dispositive on this record: petitioner pleaded only retrospective emotional-distress damages—relief unavailable under Title III and foreclosed under § 504 after Cummings—so setting aside LHEPA would not change the outcome or secure any remedy Congress made privately enforceable here. Consistent with our rights–remedies separation, we should not decide in the abstract whether LHEPA could be invoked against properly pleaded prospective injunctive relief or cognizable compensatory damages; that question is better left to a case presenting an actual conflict. I would therefore affirm on the remedial/vehicle ground, while making clear the holding is limited and does not endorse state-law alteration of federal elements when an available federal remedy is at stake.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor argue that LHEPA functions as an extra, state-law fault element that impermissibly rewrites the federal ADA/§ 504 standard of liability, regardless of remedy. But we are not obliged to decide that structural Supremacy Clause question in a case where the plaintiff has not identified any federally authorized private relief that LHEPA actually forecloses on these pleadings—Title III does not authorize private damages, and after Cummings the emotional-distress damages sought under § 504 are unavailable, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize. Absent a concrete displacement of a congressionally conferred remedy “and on what terms,” pronouncing a broad reverse-Erie rule here would be advisory and would disregard ordinary threshold principles. If a future plaintiff properly seeks prospective injunctive relief (or other clearly available relief) and a State invokes LHEPA to defeat it, that case—not this one—would warrant addressing whether the Constitution or Congress permits such a state-law overlay.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the best point that a State may not "rewrite" the elements of a federal cause of action by grafting on a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct requirement, and our reverse-Erie cases reflect that principle. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett explain, this case does not present a concrete displacement of any federally authorized private remedy: Title III does not allow private damages, and Cummings forecloses the emotional-distress damages sought under § 504, while petitioner did not pursue prospective relief. In that posture, resolving a broad Supremacy Clause question would be untethered to an actually available federal right-and-remedy pairing and risks an advisory opinion that could unsettle Congress’s reticulated remedial choices. I would affirm on the threshold remedial/vehicle ground and leave any preemption question for a case where a plaintiff seeks federally available relief and LHEPA is outcome-determinative.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas are right that petitioner’s pleaded remedies look unavailable under Title III and, after Cummings, under § 504, but that does not eliminate the Supremacy Clause problem Louisiana created by using LHEPA as a threshold condition on the existence of federal discrimination liability. The ADA and § 504 turn on Congress’s chosen causal language (“on the basis of,” “by reason of”), not an extra state-imposed gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element; allowing States to add that prerequisite would rewrite federal elements and, in practice, risk nullifying Congress’s access mandate precisely when emergency measures heighten exclusion. Our reverse-Erie cases (as Justice Kagan notes) do not permit a State to condition adjudication of a federal right on special state-law immunities, even if the remedy must ultimately be cabined under federal law on remand. The proper disposition is to hold LHEPA cannot alter the substantive standard for ADA/§ 504 claims, while leaving the remedial availability question to be addressed under federal doctrine.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas make the best vehicle point: petitioner pleaded damages largely unavailable under Title III and, after Cummings, under § 504, so a merits ruling could be unnecessary. But that framing collapses a Supremacy Clause problem into remedies: Louisiana invoked LHEPA as a heightened culpability prerequisite to liability itself, not as a post-liability limit on a particular form of relief, and our Howlett/Felder/Haywood line forbids States from overlaying special immunities or extra elements that narrow a federal right in their courts. Even if the only private remedy ultimately available is prospective relief, the State still may not rewrite the federal “by reason of/on the basis of” standard by demanding gross negligence or willful misconduct as a gate to adjudication. The proper course is to apply federal elements and defenses, then address remedy limits under federal law—so I remain with petitioner notwithstanding the remedial mismatch concerns emphasized by Justice Barrett.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor fairly warn that a State may not "rewrite" the elements of a federal claim by adding a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct prerequisite, and our Howlett/Felder line polices that sort of state-law obstruction. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, this case never tees up a federally available private remedy that LHEPA can be said to thwart: Title III does not authorize private damages, and after Cummings the emotional-distress damages pleaded under § 504 are unavailable, while petitioner did not pursue prospective relief. Without a live right-and-remedy pairing Congress actually made privately enforceable here, a sweeping Supremacy Clause holding would risk deciding an abstract conflict untethered to disposition. I would therefore affirm on the narrower remedial/vehicle ground and leave for another day whether LHEPA can operate as a defense to a properly pleaded claim for injunctive relief or cognizable compensatory damages.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest counterpoint: that LHEPA operates as an extra gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element and thus impermissibly rewrites the federal ADA/§ 504 standard. But under our Haywood/Howlett/Felder functional approach, the key question here is practical effect—whether the state rule operates as an immunity that actually forecloses adjudication of a federally authorized claim for an available federal remedy. As Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, petitioner pleaded only emotional-distress damages, which are unavailable under Title III and barred under § 504 after Cummings, and petitioner did not pursue prospective relief; on this record, setting aside LHEPA would not yield a federally authorized remedy, making a broad Supremacy Clause holding unnecessary and vehicle-problematic. I would affirm on the narrower remedial/vehicle ground while leaving open that a different case—seeking federally available injunctive relief or cognizable damages—could present a concrete preemption conflict.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to emphasize that a State may not rewrite the elements of a federal claim by imposing a heightened fault requirement, and our reverse-Erie cases (Howlett/Felder/Haywood) would have force in a proper posture. But as Justice Thomas stresses, this case does not present a concrete conflict between LHEPA and any federally authorized private remedy: petitioner sought retrospective emotional-distress damages, which Title III does not provide and which § 504 does not allow after Cummings, and he did not pursue prospective injunctive relief. Given that remedial mismatch, invalidating LHEPA would not change the relief available under federal law here, so deciding the broader Supremacy Clause question would be unnecessary and risks an advisory opinion untethered to an enforceable right-and-remedy pairing. I would affirm on that narrow ground and leave open whether LHEPA could be preempted in a case actually seeking federally available injunctive or compensatory relief.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the best case that LHEPA was applied as a heightened culpability gate to federal ADA/§ 504 liability—something our Howlett/Felder/Haywood line would not permit if it actually displaced a federally conferred, privately enforceable claim for available relief. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, we must first identify the concrete federal right-and-remedy pairing actually before us: on these pleadings petitioner sought only retrospective emotional-distress damages, which Title III does not authorize and which § 504 does not supply after Cummings. Without a live pursuit of federally available injunctive relief (or any other cognizable damages category), declaring LHEPA preempted here risks an advisory ruling untethered to an enforceable federal remedy. I would therefore affirm on this narrow vehicle/remedial ground while leaving open that LHEPA’s gross-negligence overlay could present a different conflict in a case properly seeking federally authorized prospective relief or damages.

John Roberts.reasoning: Louisiana’s LHEPA gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold operates here not as a remedy-specific limitation, but as a heightened fault element that effectively conditions whether a plaintiff may establish and enforce a federal ADA/§ 504 violation at all, and under the Supremacy Clause a State may not dilute congressionally created federal rights by interposing a more demanding state-law immunity standard. Respondents’ point that Title III private plaintiffs generally lack damages and that § 504 emotional-distress damages are unavailable after Cummings goes to remedies, not to whether federal liability and forward-looking relief (e.g., injunctions) remain available on the federal standard; the State cannot use an emergency-immunity regime to bar those federal claims wholesale. And because § 504’s enforcement is tied to Title VI’s incorporated remedial scheme, courts must respect the federal rights/remedies Congress supplied rather than importing a context-specific, state-created intent standard with no clear textual basis in the federal statutes. On these facts—denial of medically prescribed aquatic therapy during the declared emergency—LHEPA cannot be applied to raise the culpability threshold for the underlying federal discrimination inquiry.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I would resolve this case on statutory and remedial grounds before reaching any broader Supremacy Clause or structural-federalism questions. Title III of the ADA does not authorize private damages, and after Cummings § 504 likewise does not permit emotional-distress damages; here, petitioner pleaded only damages for past harm and did not seek prospective injunctive relief, so there is no federally authorized remedy for Louisiana’s LHEPA standard to “displace” in this posture. Absent a clear congressional decision authorizing the particular private relief petitioner seeks “and on what terms,” it is unnecessary to decide whether a state emergency-liability statute could otherwise operate as a defense to a federal claim. On these facts, any preemption holding would be advisory because petitioner’s federal claims fail regardless of LHEPA.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Starting with the operative federal texts and remedies, Title III of the ADA does not authorize private damages, and after Cummings emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504; thus, even if Louisiana’s LHEPA were set aside, petitioner’s damages theory largely fails as a matter of federal law, and the case is a poor vehicle to resolve a broad Supremacy Clause question. This Court has repeatedly been reluctant to allow alternative doctrines to expand or “swallow” a carefully limited remedial scheme, and here the federal scheme’s limited private relief makes it difficult to show that applying a state immunity threshold meaningfully displaces a federally conferred damages remedy. On these pleadings, the state court’s application of LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold does not clearly conflict with any privately available federal remedy, and petitioner has not shown entitlement to relief that federal law would otherwise provide. Accordingly, I would deny relief and vote for respondents.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III and § 504 prohibit discrimination “on the basis of” disability—text that requires a causal link, not a showing of gross negligence, willful misconduct, or improper purpose, and a State may not add extra-textual fault elements that narrow federally created rights. Applying LHEPA’s emergency-immunity threshold to these federal causes of action functions as a state-law override of the substantive standard of liability and risks eviscerating paradigmatic ADA/RA claims—especially access and reasonable-modification disputes that rarely turn on culpability—precisely when disabled individuals most need federal protections. Respondents are right that damages are constrained (Title III private plaintiffs generally obtain only injunctive relief; and after Cummings emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504), but remedial limits do not authorize a State to extinguish or re-write the federal claim itself, particularly where prospective relief to prevent ongoing discrimination may still be available. Under the Supremacy Clause, Louisiana courts may apply neutral state procedural rules, but they cannot interpose a categorical or heightened-fault immunity that effectively defeats federal civil-rights enforcement in state court.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not allow a State, by labeling a rule “immunity” and tying it to an emergency declaration, to rewrite the substantive standard governing a federal cause of action litigated in state court. On this record, Louisiana courts applied LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold to ADA Title III and § 504 claims—thereby heightening the plaintiff’s burden beyond what federal law requires and effectively narrowing Congress’s chosen enforcement scheme, a move this Court has treated as impermissible under reverse-Erie principles. Even if the remedies petitioner seeks are limited (Title III generally to injunctive relief and § 504 after Cummings as to emotional-distress damages), that goes to relief on the merits, not to a State’s authority to condition federal rights on a special fault showing. The proper course is to apply the federal elements and defenses as federal law supplies them, not to import a state emergency-liability regime that “constrains” federally conferred antidiscrimination protections.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Start with the enacted remedial scheme Congress chose. Title III of the ADA authorizes private plaintiffs only to seek injunctive relief, and § 504 (a Spending Clause statute) after Cummings does not allow the emotional-distress damages the petitioner principally seeks—so on this record the state court’s resort to LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold does not meaningfully "displace" a federally available remedy so much as operate in a field where the requested federal relief is unavailable anyway. And because the question presented is whether LHEPA can "effectively bar" these claims in state court, the petitioner has not shown that federal law clearly supplies the relief necessary to make LHEPA outcome-determinative here. Given our obligation to decide no more than necessary, I would deny relief and leave for another day any broader Supremacy Clause holding about state emergency-immunity statutes where a plaintiff seeks a form of relief Congress unmistakably made available.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the Haywood/Howlett/Felder framework, the key question is whether Louisiana’s LHEPA operates in practice as an “immunity statute cloaked in jurisdictional garb” that forecloses a merits resolution of a defined category of federal claims. On these pleadings, the petitioner sought only emotional-distress damages and did not pursue forward-looking injunctive relief; but Title III of the ADA does not allow private damages, and Cummings holds emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504, so LHEPA’s heightened fault threshold does not, in effect, immunize defendants from any federally authorized remedy in this case. Because there is no viable federal damages remedy to be displaced and no alleged catch-22 preventing adjudication of an available federal remedy, this case is a poor vehicle to extend Haywood/Howlett/Felder beyond § 1983 or to decide a broader preemption question in the abstract. If a future case squarely presented a state immunity rule that actually blocked an available federal remedy (e.g., injunctive relief or properly pleaded compensatory damages), the Supremacy Clause analysis could be different.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A straightforward application of controlling remedial precedent substantially narrows what is even at stake: Title III private plaintiffs may obtain only injunctive relief, and after Cummings emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504, so petitioner’s state-court complaint seeking only emotional-distress damages does not identify a federally authorized remedy that Louisiana’s LHEPA could be said to “thwart.” Under our threshold-focused approach, that remedial defect is dispositive before reaching any broader Supremacy Clause question about whether a state emergency-immunity regime may heighten the fault standard for a federal cause of action. On this record, LHEPA functions (at most) as a limit on state-law “civil liability” in damages during the emergency, not as a categorical bar to the federally available injunctive relief that remains the core private enforcement mechanism under Title III (and potentially § 504). Because the case is thus a poor vehicle for deciding any reverse-Erie/preemption issue, I would vote to deny relief and affirm for respondents.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Using traditional tools of interpretation, I would first identify what federal law actually makes enforceable here: Title III authorizes private suits for injunctive relief (not damages), and § 504—construed under our Spending Clause remedial precedents—does not permit the emotional-distress damages petitioner principally seeks after Cummings. Given those remedial limits, the state court’s application of LHEPA’s heightened culpability threshold does not clearly operate to displace a federally conferred damages remedy in this case, and petitioner has not shown a concrete, available federal remedy that LHEPA categorically nullifies on these pleadings. While our Supremacy Clause cases (e.g., Felder/Howlett/Haywood) forbid state-law immunities that effectively defeat federal causes of action in state court, this record does not present that clean conflict because the relief sought is largely unavailable as a matter of federal law and the remaining injunctive claim is not shown to be foreclosed by LHEPA’s fault standard. On this posture, I would not grant relief against the state-court judgment or set a broad preemption rule untethered to an actually enforceable federal right and remedy in these particular facts.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Louisiana’s COVID-era health-emergency immunity statute (LHEPA) can be applied in state court to heighten the fault standard (gross negligence/willful misconduct) or otherwise bar enforcement of federal disability-rights causes of action under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Louisiana Health Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA) immunity provisions (as applied during the declared COVID-19 public health emergency), and the federal antidiscrimination statutes: Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues Louisiana courts improperly used LHEPA—a state emergency-liability immunity rule designed to protect healthcare providers from ordinary negligence suits during a declared emergency—to defeat or materially alter federal civil-rights claims under the ADA and Rehabilitation Act. According to petitioner, importing LHEPA’s heightened culpability requirement (gross negligence/willful misconduct) into federal statutory claims changes the elements of the federal causes of action, makes federal rights contingent on state emergency declarations, and is preempted under the Supremacy Clause because it obstructs Congress’s objectives of uniform, nationwide enforcement of disability nondiscrimination standards and remedies. Petitioner also emphasizes that the Louisiana Supreme Court denied review on immunity grounds without reaching the merits, and that the First Circuit treated the federal claims through LHEPA’s lens simply because the denial of requested aquatic therapy occurred during the COVID emergency, producing 'absurd' results and dangerous precedent for future emergencies.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue certiorari should be denied because petitioner’s damages theory is legally unavailable regardless of LHEPA. They contend the petition rests on an incorrect premise that petitioner could obtain compensatory emotional-distress damages under Title III of the ADA or § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act in a private action. They point to controlling federal precedent limiting remedies: Title III generally does not permit private-party damages, and § 504 does not allow emotional-distress damages (per Cummings). Respondents also invoke the state-court rulings that petitioner at most alleged ordinary negligence, not the gross negligence or willful misconduct required to overcome LHEPA immunity during the declared public health emergency, and they note the Louisiana appellate court characterized petitioner’s preemption arguments as conclusory and unsupported. In short, respondents frame the case as a poor vehicle and not outcome-determinative on the federal question because the requested monetary relief is unavailable under federal law anyway.
key_precedents: Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. ___ (2022)
Mills v. Hartford Healthcare Corp., 347 A.3d 605 (Conn. 2023)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett press a serious vehicle/redressability concern: if Title III affords only prospective relief and Cummings narrows §504 damages, setting aside LHEPA may not change petitioner’s ultimate recovery. But that point goes to remedies, not to whether Louisiana may add a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element that the ADA and §504 do not contain; as Justice Kagan notes, the state courts used LHEPA as a merits filter to defeat the federal claims at the threshold. Under Felder and Howlett, a State may not interpose an immunity-like heightened-fault overlay that functionally “restricts or limits” the federal right, even if the remaining federal relief is limited to injunctions and fees. The appropriate course is to hold the LHEPA overlay preempted as applied to the federal causes of action and remand for the lower courts to determine which federal remedies are available on the pleadings and record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Felder and Howlett identifies a serious general principle: a State ordinarily may not superadd an immunity-like heightened-fault element to defeat a federal cause of action. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Alito emphasize, we must first determine whether setting aside LHEPA would yield any congressionally authorized, redressable relief on this record—Title III generally affords only prospective injunctive relief (plus fees), and Cummings substantially narrows §504 damages, while petitioner principally pursued retrospective compensatory damages. Absent a clear, live request for prospective relief that LHEPA actually foreclosed, reaching a broad Supremacy Clause holding would decide an unnecessary constitutional question untethered to the judgment. I would therefore resolve the case on the antecedent remedial/vehicle ground and leave the preemption question for a case where the state overlay demonstrably blocks available federal relief.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan are right to stress, under Felder and Howlett, that a State ordinarily may not graft an immunity-like heightened-culpability element onto a federal cause of action. But Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett persuasively identify an antecedent redressability/vehicle defect: petitioner’s case, as litigated, largely sought retrospective damages that Title III generally does not authorize and that § 504 cannot supply as emotional-distress damages after Cummings, and the record does not clearly present a live request for prospective relief that LHEPA uniquely defeated. In that posture, announcing a broad Supremacy Clause holding risks deciding a constitutional question unnecessary to the judgment and untethered to demonstrable relief. The sound course is to deny relief/affirm on the remedial-posture ground and leave the preemption question for a case where a congressionally available remedy is plainly blocked by the state overlay.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett’s vehicle/redressability concern is serious, but it mischaracterizes what the Louisiana courts did: they did not merely limit remedies; they used LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold to defeat the federal ADA and § 504 claims on the merits by adding an element Congress did not require. Under Felder and Howlett—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize—a State may not interpose an immunity-like overlay that “restricts or limits” federally created rights, even if the remaining relief is prospective injunctions and fees. The uncertainty about the scope of available federal remedies after Cummings goes to what relief follows a finding of liability, not to whether a State may rewrite the liability standard; the correct course is to hold the LHEPA overlay preempted as applied and remand for the lower courts to apply the federal standards and then determine remedies.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett have the strongest point on vehicle/redressability—if no federal remedy is available, we should avoid a broad Supremacy Clause ruling. But the state courts used LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct screen to defeat the ADA and § 504 claims at the threshold, thereby altering the federally supplied elements of a violation rather than merely trimming remedies; under Felder and Howlett, that kind of immunity-like overlay is preempted even if the plaintiff also sought forms of relief federal law may not ultimately permit. Chief Justice Roberts is right to separate liability from remedy: we can hold the LHEPA overlay preempted as applied to these federal causes of action and remand for the lower courts to determine, under Title III and Cummings, what relief (injunction, fees, or otherwise) remains. Deciding the case on the “no damages anyway” ground would leave in place a state-law merits filter that risks nullifying federal disability-rights standards during emergencies—the very context in which Congress and the expert agencies recognized heightened access risks.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan are right that, under Felder and Howlett, a State may not superadd an immunity-like culpability element that rewrites the merits of a federal cause of action. But Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett correctly insist on an antecedent, case-dispositive question: whether petitioner has identified any congressionally authorized, redressable remedy that the LHEPA overlay actually foreclosed on this record, given Title III’s usual limitation to prospective relief and Cummings’s narrowing of damages under § 504. If setting aside LHEPA would not change the available relief or the judgment because the pleaded remedies are unavailable as a matter of federal law, then a broad Supremacy Clause holding would be unnecessary and risk an advisory constitutional pronouncement. The restrained course is to resolve this case on the remedial/vehicle ground and leave the preemption question for a case where a live request for prospective relief (or other available relief) was clearly defeated by the state overlay.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Felder/Howlett point is the strongest for petitioner: a State generally cannot superadd an immunity-like gross-negligence element that functionally rewrites federal liability, and Justice Kagan is right that this concerns elements, not merely remedies. But Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett persuasively identify an antecedent vehicle/redressability problem—on this record petitioner primarily sought retrospective damages that Title III typically does not authorize for private plaintiffs and that § 504 cannot supply as emotional-distress damages after Cummings—so it is unclear that invalidating LHEPA would change the judgment. Given our preference for deciding cases on narrower, nonconstitutional grounds and avoiding advisory Supremacy Clause pronouncements, I would resolve this case on the remedial/posture ground and leave the important preemption question for a cleaner case where clearly available prospective relief was actually foreclosed. That course is more institutionally modest and more workable in future emergency-immunity contexts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan are right that, in the abstract, Felder/Howlett forbid a State from superadding an immunity-like element that alters the liability standard for a federal claim. But that merits principle does not warrant decision here unless setting aside LHEPA would likely change the outcome by opening a congressionally authorized, live form of relief on this record; as Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, petitioner primarily pursued damages that Title III generally does not provide and that Cummings largely forecloses as emotional-distress damages under § 504. Without a clearly pleaded, still-available request for prospective relief that LHEPA uniquely defeated, a broad preemption holding risks an unnecessary constitutional ruling divorced from redressability. The narrower course is to resolve on the remedial/vehicle ground and leave the Supremacy Clause question for a case where the state overlay demonstrably blocks available federal relief.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan are right that, as a general matter, Felder and Howlett forbid States from superadding an immunity-like heightened-fault element that functionally rewrites a federal cause of action. But Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett persuasively press the antecedent, case-dispositive question whether any congressionally authorized, redressable relief was actually available and uniquely foreclosed by LHEPA on this record, given Title III’s usual prospective-relief limitation and Cummings’s narrowing of damages under § 504. Using traditional tools of restraint, I am not prepared to announce a broad Supremacy Clause rule about emergency-immunity overlays where the petitioner’s pleaded, live federal remedy is uncertain and the asserted conflict may be outcome-irrelevant. The more judicially modest course is to deny relief here and leave the preemption merits for a cleaner vehicle where the state overlay demonstrably blocks an available federal remedy.

John Roberts.reasoning: The starting point is the federal statutes’ text: Title III and § 504 create federal nondiscrimination duties and supply federal enforcement mechanisms, and nothing in their language conditions liability on a state-declared emergency or imposes a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct element. Applying LHEPA in state court to raise the culpability threshold effectively rewrites the elements of the federal causes of action and “restrict[s] or limit[s]” the federally conferred rights and remedies by making their enforceability turn on state immunity policy rather than Congress’s commands, which the Supremacy Clause does not allow. Respondents’ remedy-based objections (e.g., limits on damages under Title III and Cummings) may narrow the relief available, but they do not justify a state-law rule that categorically heightens the federal liability standard and blocks adjudication of the underlying federal violation. Under the Spending Clause notice framework, funding recipients are on notice of § 504’s federal conditions and the attendant federal enforcement scheme; they are not on notice that state emergency-immunity statutes can dilute those obligations by importing an extra-statutory fault element into federal law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Before reaching any Supremacy Clause or preemption question about Louisiana’s LHEPA, I would first determine what federal law actually authorizes by way of a private cause of action and remedies. Here, the petitioner’s state-court pleading seeks emotional-distress/compensatory damages for a past denial of therapy, but Title III of the ADA affords private plaintiffs only prospective injunctive relief (and fees), and this Court in Cummings held emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504’s Spending Clause remedial scheme; on these facts, LHEPA’s heightened culpability standard for money-damages liability is not outcome-determinative as to any remedy Congress made available. Given that threshold statutory-remedy defect (and the apparent absence of any pleaded claim for prospective injunctive relief), prudential restraint counsels against deciding the broader constitutional question whether a State’s emergency-immunity rule may be applied to alter the elements of a federal disability-discrimination claim in state court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: This case presents serious Supremacy Clause questions, but it is a poor vehicle for resolving them because it is not clear the asserted federal remedies are available even if LHEPA drops out: Title III generally does not authorize private compensatory damages, and emotional-distress damages under § 504 are foreclosed by Cummings, so the state immunity overlay may not be outcome-determinative on the relief petitioner seeks. Consistent with my usual approach, I would not reach a broad and potentially disruptive preemption holding about how state emergency-immunity regimes interact with the ADA/RA without a clean merits posture and a record showing what concrete federal relief remains (e.g., injunctive relief) and whether LHEPA was properly applied to it. Where the dispositive remedial and preservation questions are murky and the statutory interaction is “devilishly difficult,” the appropriate course is to deny relief rather than announce a sweeping rule that could unsettle reticulated federal and state enforcement schemes. On this record, petitioner has not shown that LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard actually barred a viable federal cause of action with available relief.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The operative federal texts—Title III’s prohibition on discrimination in public accommodations and § 504’s ban on exclusion “solely by reason of” disability—do not condition liability on “gross negligence” or “willful misconduct,” and a State may not, by relabeling a heightened culpability threshold as emergency “immunity,” effectively add elements that Congress did not require. Applied here, LHEPA makes the availability of federal disability-rights enforcement turn on a State’s emergency declaration and elevates the plaintiff’s burden beyond what the ADA and § 504 demand, a practical effect that would shrink or nullify paradigmatic claims (including denials of necessary modifications/accommodations during emergencies), thereby obstructing Congress’s uniform, nationwide scheme. Under reverse-Erie/Supremacy Clause principles, state rules that functionally defeat federal causes of action in state court are preempted, and the state-court disposition appears to have treated the federal claims through LHEPA’s lens rather than adjudicating the federal elements on their own terms. Respondents’ remedial arguments (limits on private damages under Title III and Cummings’s bar on emotional-distress damages under § 504) do not cure the preemption problem because States still may not impose immunity barriers that foreclose whatever federal relief remains available (including injunctive and other authorized remedies).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, Louisiana cannot condition the enforcement of federal ADA Title III and Rehabilitation Act § 504 rights on a state-declared emergency by importing LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard, because that effectively rewrites the elements Congress chose for those federal causes of action and creates a state-law immunity-like obstacle to the federal scheme. As in Felder and Howlett, a State may not use its own liability-limiting rules to single out (or functionally defeat) federal civil-rights claims in its courts when Congress has supplied the governing standards and remedies. The deliberate-omission principle reinforces that conclusion: Congress specified when heightened intent (e.g., “deliberate indifference” for damages under § 504/ADA) is required, and state courts cannot superadd a different culpability threshold that Congress did not enact. Respondents’ remedial arguments (limits on damages under Title III and Cummings) may affect available relief, but they do not authorize a State to bar or dilute the underlying federal right (including injunctive relief and any otherwise-available remedies) via a state emergency-immunity overlay.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Start with the federal texts and their remedial schemes: Title III of the ADA generally authorizes private injunctive relief rather than damages, and after Cummings § 504 does not permit emotional-distress damages, so petitioner’s theory that LHEPA “defeats” those monetary remedies appears largely beside the point on these facts. Even accepting the petitioner’s Supremacy Clause framing under cases like Felder/Howlett (state immunity rules cannot nullify federal rights), the record as described suggests Louisiana’s application of LHEPA goes to shielding providers from damages liability during the emergency, not to closing the courthouse to the federal claim for prospective relief. Given the apparent remedy mismatch and vehicle problems (state courts focused on lack of gross negligence; damages sought that federal law does not supply), I would not use this case to announce a broad preemption rule about emergency immunities’ interaction with ADA/§ 504 claims. The separation-of-powers virtues of rule-like limits counsel resolving the case on the narrower, controlling remedial ground rather than expanding federal enforcement through a preemption holding unnecessary to the outcome.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s Supremacy Clause precedents, a State generally may not apply a state-law immunity or heightened fault rule in a way that effectively nullifies or discriminates against a federal cause of action in its courts. But this case is a poor vehicle to decide the broad preemption question because, on these specific facts, the relief petitioner principally seeks (compensatory/emotional-distress damages) is largely unavailable under federal law in any event—Title III typically authorizes only injunctive relief for private plaintiffs, and § 504 does not permit emotional-distress damages. Given those remedy limits and the state courts’ determination that the complaint alleged at most ordinary negligence rather than intentional or egregious misconduct, I would not use this case to announce a new rule about emergency-immunity statutes and federal disability-rights enforcement. Respect for precedent, workability, and judicial restraint counsel denying petitioner relief here and leaving any broader Supremacy Clause clarification for a case where the federal claim and remedy are clearly viable and outcome-determinative.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I would start with the precise doctrinal prerequisite: whether this case cleanly presents an outcome-determinative Supremacy Clause question given the remedies actually available under the asserted federal causes of action. On this record, petitioner sought monetary relief, but Title III of the ADA generally does not allow private damages, and under Cummings emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504; that mismatch means petitioner has not shown that setting aside LHEPA would redress his injury in this vehicle. Because the asserted federal question (whether LHEPA may heighten the fault standard or bar the federal claims) is not shown to be dispositive of the judgment—independent remedial limits would still defeat the requested relief—this is a poor fit for resolving the preemption issue. Consistent with my insistence on clear doctrinal fit and record-grounded proof before reaching merits, I would vote to deny relief and leave the broader preemption question for a case in which a plaintiff seeks and can obtain an available federal remedy (e.g., properly pleaded prospective injunctive relief).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying traditional tools of construction and the Court’s Supremacy Clause cases, a State generally may not use a state-law immunity or heightened-fault rule to negate or alter the elements of a federal cause of action, because state courts must entertain federal claims on terms that do not discriminate against or obstruct federal rights. But on this record, respondents’ remedy-based arguments substantially undercut the case as an outcome-determinative vehicle: Title III of the ADA largely forecloses private damages, and § 504 does not permit emotional-distress damages after Cummings, so petitioner has not shown that the LHEPA gross-negligence overlay actually changed the availability of the federal relief she can obtain. Given those remedial limits and the state courts’ findings that the pleadings alleged, at most, ordinary negligence during the declared emergency, I would not reach a broad preemption holding in a posture where the federal question may not affect the ultimate disposition. Consistent with preservation and restraint principles, this case is a poor vehicle to decide the scope of preemption for state emergency-immunity statutes as applied to federal disability-rights claims.
